sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:1
items.html:
It explains: The matter of the coupling by striking, which comprises two forces, the drawing force and the repelling force, acting at once, this in the coarseness and that in the hardness in the screen.

A broad explanation of the words “coupling by striking”
And the above matter of the coupling by striking requires a broad explanation, for it seems at first that there is here a meaning of affirmation and negation together, since a coupling and a striking mean, on their face, rejection and separation and great hatred, so how can one speak of a “coupling of striking,” whose meaning would be a love of hatred, or an attachment of separation, or a drawing of rejection, which seems very perplexing at first.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:2
items.html: However it is indeed so, that these are two opposites under a single dominion, except that this dominion is composed of two distinct subjects, namely two forces: the drawing force and the repelling force, where the drawing force rests in the coarseness of the vessel, and the repelling force rests in the screen that is in the vessel, which are combined one with the other, and both rule at once, at the same time, in two places.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:3
items.html: And in order to clarify this well, so it will be accepted by the mind without arousing any wonder or confusion, I will elaborate somewhat, and give you a parable from the imagined corporeal reality that is plain to our eyes. For example, when you see a stone or a man falling from a high place to the ground, it appears to your eyes that the man is drawn from above downward with great strength and great speed, and yet, when he reaches and touches the ground, the ground strikes him, and repels him somewhat upward.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:4
items.html: And there are two opinions here. One opinion is that the earth has a great drawing force toward everything placed in the air of the sky, if it has nothing solid to protect it. Therefore, when a person moves, for instance, from the roof of a house into the air, the drawing force of the earth immediately rules over him. And by this they explain the matter of falling at great speed to the ground. However there is a difficulty here, for according to this the earth should have to embrace him with great love, so that he could not move from it even a hair's breadth for a moment. Yet we see the opposite, for the very first moment he touches it, it immediately repels him with speed, and he returns a little backward, upward.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:5
items.html: And against this there is another opinion, that there is some kind of repelling force from above, from the air of our earth, whereby the repelling force acts on everything found in the air, repelling it toward our earth. And our earth too has only the repelling force, and nothing at all of the drawing force. Therefore, when a person moves from the roof of a house and comes into the air of the sky, the repelling force from above acts on him at once and brings him down to the earth, and so when he touches the earth, it again repels him backward, upward.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:6
items.html: However, if we trace the branch to its root in the upper worlds, where for the most part the matters are close to one another, we find that these two opinions are not correct, and it is possible to say here too, that every sphere has a drawing force and a repelling force combined with one another, that is, there is there a coarseness force, which is a drawing force, to draw within it everything that is outside it. And opposite it, it has a hardness force, which repels from it every external body from entering into it. Therefore, every drawing is certainly from the force of the central point in its internality, since there the drawing force within it rests, since the central point is coarser than the whole sphere, and therefore it draws to itself everything found within the circumferential space that lies under the force of its action and dominion.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:7
items.html: Yet it does not draw the thing to the point of swallowing it, as would be obligatory from the aspect of its drawing force alone, but rather, at the very moment the thing being drawn touches its outer shell, the repelling force resting in its shell, which is the hardness, immediately awakens, and repels it back upward.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:8
items.html: And it follows that the thing it drew to itself comes to be received, but not in the manner of its drawing, but in another manner, since it is stopped midway, because of the hardness and repelling force that restrains it on its way, as explained. Thus a coupling and a striking act here together, whereby the coupling is the drawing, and the hardness is the repelling, whereby it thus receives it unto itself and does not swallow it alive into its belly. Accordingly it is possible to say that the essence of the vessel of reception is the repelling force within it, which receives it and holds it as is fitting to be, for were it not for the repelling force, it would be swallowed alive into it.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:9
items.html: You will also see that the drawing and the repelling are equal to one another, like two drops of water, in the measure of their strength: for if the drawing force were slightly greater than the repelling force, there would be no possibility at all of moving upon it, since whatever moved on it would stick to it, like iron to a magnet stone. And if the repelling force were slightly greater, then the whole universe would dance upon it and could not touch it at all. Hence they are equal.

items.sefariaRef: Talmud Eser HaSefirot, Section II, Histaklut Penimit 10:10
items.html: And in this manner you will well understand the matter of the coupling by striking that operates in the upper ones, whereby although the coupling and the striking are two opposites, nevertheless they share one dominion, at once, at the same time, except in two places, which are the coarseness and the hardness, as above. And remember this for the entire continuation of this wisdom.
